questions.q: What did Absalom prepare for himself?
questions.a: Absalom prepared a chariot and horses for himself.

questions.q: Who ran before Absalom’s chariot?
questions.a: He hired fifty men to run in front of his chariot.

questions.q: Whom would Absalom call to as he stood by the gate?
questions.a: Absalom would call to any man who had a dispute and was coming to the king for judgment.

questions.q: What would Absalom say about the cases of the men who came for judgment?
questions.a: Absalom would say to them that their matter was good and right, but the king is not able to decide everyone’s case, and he has not appointed anyone else to judge cases for people like you.

questions.q: Why did Absalom say he wished he were a judge in the land?
questions.a: Absalom said he wished he were a judge so that every person with a dispute could come to him and he would give them justice.

questions.q: What did Absalom do when a man approached to prostrate himself?
questions.a: Absalom would stretch out his hand, hold the man up, and kiss him on the cheek.

questions.q: What did Absalom steal from the men of Israel?
questions.a: Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel. The Israelites began to wish that Absalom were their king instead of David.

questions.q: What reason did Absalom give the king for needing to go to Hebron?
questions.a: Absalom said he had to go to Hebron to fulfill a vow he had made to Yahweh.

questions.q: What did the spies that Absalom sent throughout Israel say?
questions.a: The spies said that when people heard the sound of the shofar, they should say that Absalom has become the king at Hebron.

questions.q: Did the two hundred men who went with Absalom to Hebron know of his plans?
questions.a: No, the two hundred men came because he had invited them to the feast he was going to host there. They were not part of his conspiracy. They knew nothing about what he was planning to do.

questions.q: What did David tell his servants to do after a messenger told him that the hearts of the men of Israel were behind Absalom?
questions.a: David told his servants in Jerusalem to arise and flee, because there would be no escape from Absalom.

questions.q: Whom did the king leave behind in Jerusalem to keep the house?
questions.a: The king left ten women, who were concubines, to keep the house.

questions.q: Who marched with the king as he left Jerusalem?
questions.a: All his servants, all the Cherethites, all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites—600 men from Gath—marched with him.

questions.q: What did Ittai the Gittite tell the king after the king told him to return?
questions.a: Ittai swore that he would go wherever the king would go, and he would fight to defend David even if he had to die doing that.

questions.q: Which way did David and all those with him go as they left Jerusalem?
questions.a: Since Absalom would be coming from the southwest, the king and the others crossed the Kidron Valley and then went up the hill on the road that goes through the desolate area east of Jerusalem.

questions.q: What did the king tell Zadok the priest to do with the Box of God?
questions.a: The king told Zadok to take the Box of God back to the city.

questions.q: Why was David going to wait at the fords of the wilderness?
questions.a: He was going to wait there until a word came from the priests to tell him what to do.

questions.q: What did David pray when he was told that Ahithophel was with Absalom?
questions.a: David prayed that Yahweh would make Ahithophel give Absalom bad advice.

questions.q: Who did David meet at the top of the Mount of Olives?
questions.a: David unexpectedly met Hushai the Archite, who had torn his clothes and put dirt on his head to show that he was very sad.

questions.q: What did David want Hushai the Archite to do for him?
questions.a: David wanted Hushai to return to the city and offer to be Absalom’s servant so he would be able to counter any good advice that Ahithophel would give to Absalom.

questions.q: To whom did David want Hushai to report everything he heard in the king’s palace?
questions.a: David wanted Hushai to report everything to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.

commentary.text: Verses 1–6 David allows Absalom's pomp. Those parents know not what they do, who indulge a proud humour in their children: many young people are ruined by pride. And those commonly are most eager for authority who least understand its duties.

See how willing tender parents are to believe the best concerning their children. But how easy and how wicked is it, for children to take advantage of good parents, and to deceive them with the show of religion! The principal men of Jerusalem joined Absalom's feast upon his sacrifice. Pious persons are glad to see others appear religious, and this gives occasion for deceptions. The policy of wicked men, and the subtlety of Satan, are exerted to draw good persons to countenance base designs.

David determined to quit Jerusalem. He took this resolve, as a penitent submitting to the rod. Before unrighteous Absalom he could justify himself, and stand out; but before the righteous God he must condemn himself, and yield to his judgments. Thus he accepts the punishment of his sin. And good men, when they themselves suffer, are anxious that others should not be led to suffer with them. He compelled none; those whose hearts were with Absalom, to Absalom let them go, and so shall their doom be. Thus Christ enlists none but willing followers. David cannot bear to think that Ittai, a stranger and an exile, a proselyte and a new convert, who ought to be encouraged and made easy, should meet with hard usage. But such value has Ittai for David's wisdom and goodness, that he will not leave him. He is a friend indeed, who loves at all times, and will adhere to us in adversity. Let us cleave to the Son of David, with full purpose of heart, and neither life nor death shall separate us from his love.

David is very careful for the safety of the ark. It is right to be more concerned for the church's prosperity than our own; to prefer the success of the gospel above our own wealth, credit, ease, and safety. Observe with what satisfaction and submission David speaks of the Divine disposal. It is our interest, as well as our duty, cheerfully to acquiesce in the will of God, whatever befalls us. Let us see God's hand in all events; and that we may not be afraid of what shall be, let us see all events in God's hand. David's sin was ever before him, Ps 51:3; but never so plain, nor ever appearing so black as now. He never wept thus when Saul hunted him, but a wounded conscience makes troubles lie heavy, Ps 38:4.

David prays not against Ahithophel's person, but against his counsel. He prayed this, in firm belief that God has all hearts in his hand, and tongues also. But we must second our prayers with endeavours, and David did so, else we tempt God. But we do not find wisdom and simplicity so united in any mere man, that we can perceive nothing which needs forgiveness. Yet, when the Son of David was treated with all possible treachery and cruelty, his wisdom, meekness, candour, and patience, were perfect. Him let us follow, cleave to, and serve, in life and in death.
